title: もの and こと: advanced uses
summary: もの is a noun, a thing, even an abstract one. こと is a fact or state of affairs: したことがある, することがある, and sentence-ending ものだ.

blocks.text: The usual advice says **もの** is concrete (a pencil) and **こと** abstract (a situation). That is a fine start, but it breaks down. What もの really means is **a thing**, a noun: it can be an apple or it can be love. **こと** is a **state of affairs**, a fact, something that happens or exists.

blocks.jp: 愛は素晴らしいものだ。
blocks.en: Love is a wonderful thing. (love is a noun, a thing)

blocks.text: ことがある: the fact exists

Japanese has no separate perfect tense. It says that **the fact of having done it exists**. Put the verb in the **past** and you have experience; put it in the **present** and you have something that sometimes happens.

blocks.jp: 日本に行ったことがある。
blocks.en: I have been to Japan. (the fact of having gone exists)

blocks.jp: 日本に行くことがある。
blocks.en: I sometimes go to Japan. (the fact of going exists)

blocks.jp: 誰でも失敗することがある。

blocks.text: The tense is what matters. Compare the same place with the same helper, in two memories:

blocks.jp: 東京に行ったことがある。
blocks.en: I have been to Tokyo. (a plain fact of experience)

blocks.jp: 東京によく行ったものだ。
blocks.en: I used to go to Tokyo a lot. (a fond memory)

blocks.text: ものだ as a sentence ender

Adding **ものだ** to a full sentence turns it into a **thing**: a reality you have to accept, "that's just how it is". The generalization has to be in the present. In the **past**, **〜たものだ** becomes a personal memory: "I used to...", with feeling.

blocks.en: Winter is cold, that's just how it is.

blocks.jp: 人は誰でも間違えるものだ。
blocks.en: Everyone makes mistakes. (that's just how people are)

blocks.jp: 子供のころ、よくここに来たものだ。
blocks.en: As a child I used to come here often.

rows: 行ったことがある: have done it
行くことがある: sometimes happens
行ったものだ: used to, with feeling
行くものだ: that's how it is

blocks.text: At the end of a written rule or notice, **こと** states what has been decided: "the matter is that you do this". It is a rule (like a 決まり, cf. ことにする in lesson 29), not an order from one person to another.

blocks.en: Hand in your homework without fail.

blocks.jp: 動物にえさをやらないこと。
blocks.en: Do not feed the animals. (a sign)

items: **もの**: a thing (any noun, concrete or abstract).
**こと**: a fact or situation. **〜たことがある** = have done; **〜ることがある** = sometimes happens.
**〜ものだ** (present) = that's how it is; **〜たものだ** = used to, with feeling.
Rules and notices can end in **こと**: it states a decided rule, not a personal command.

questions.instruction: Which sentence says "I have (once) eaten sushi"?
options: すしを食べることがある。
すしを食べたことがある。
すしを食べたものがある。
questions.note: Past verb + ことがある = the fact of having done it exists.

questions.prompt: 朝ごはんを食べないことがある。
options: There are times when (I) don't eat breakfast
questions.en: There are times when (I) don't eat breakfast.
questions.note: Present tense + ことがある = it sometimes happens.

questions.prompt: 一度もパンダを見た＿＿がない。
questions.en: I have never seen a panda.
questions.note: たことがない: the fact of having done it does not exist.

questions.prompt: 年を取ると、体が弱くなる＿＿だ。
questions.en: As you get older, the body gets weaker; that's just how it is.
questions.note: Present ものだ states how things are.

questions.prompt: 学生のころ、毎日この道を歩いた＿＿だ。
questions.en: When I was a student, I used to walk this road every day.
questions.note: Past たものだ is a personal memory: I used to.

questions.prompt: ここでは大きい声を出さない＿＿。
questions.en: Do not raise your voice here.
questions.note: こと at the end of a written rule is a firm instruction.

questions.instruction: Which sentence is a general "that's how it is"?
options: 子供のころ、よく泣いたものだ。
日本へ行ったことがある。
questions.note: Present ものだ states reality; past たものだ is a memory.
In the past, ものだ turns into a memory with feeling.

questions.instruction: What does もの really mean?
options: A thing, a noun (concrete or abstract)
questions.note: もの can be an apple or love.

options: A fact or state of affairs
questions.note: こと is something that happens or exists.

questions.instruction: True or false? A past verb + ことがある means "have done".
questions.note: The fact of having done it exists.

questions.instruction: Tap the word whose tense makes this an experience
questions.note: The past 住んだ before ことがある gives "have done".

questions.instruction: Tap the word that turns the sentence into an order
questions.note: こと at the end of a rule is a firm instruction.
Present verb + ことがある = it sometimes happens.
Past verb + ことがない = never.

questions.prompt: Children love to play; that's just how it is.
questions.en: Children love to play; that's just how it is.
questions.note: Present ものだ states a reality to accept.

questions.prompt: When I was little, I used to swim every day.
questions.en: When I was little, I used to swim every day.
questions.note: Past たものだ is a nostalgic "used to".

questions.instruction: True or false? もの can only be a physical object.
questions.note: もの is a noun: it can be an apple or love.

questions.instruction: Which sentence is a written rule on a notice?
options: 廊下を走ったことがある。
廊下を走ることがある。
questions.note: こと at the end is a firm instruction.

questions.instruction: Why can ことがある mean both "have done" and "sometimes does"?
options: The tense of the verb before it changes the meaning
questions.note: Past gives experience; present gives something that sometimes happens.

questions.prompt: ここで写真をとった＿＿がありますか。
questions.en: Have you ever taken a photo here?
questions.note: たことがある asks about experience.

questions.instruction: Which form of the verb before ことがある means "sometimes happens"?
questions.note: Present gives something that sometimes happens.
